akbar: Akbar expanded Mughal rule and strengthened imperial administration. His court brought together artists from different traditions and hosted religious discussions.
Supported Fatehpur Sikri and manuscript workshops with artists from diverse backgrounds.
His patronage helped shape a Mughal style combining Indian, Persian and European elements.
augustus: Augustus was Rome's first emperor. Official portraits presented him as youthful and dignified across the empire.
Established the first imperial reign and used official imagery to communicate his authority.
His portraits became a model for linking a ruler's image with political messaging.
franklin: Benjamin Franklin arrived in France in 1776 to seek support for American independence.
Served as a congressional commissioner and helped advance the 1778 alliance with France.
His diplomacy connected the American cause with French support.
gudea: Gudea ruled Lagash in southern Mesopotamia. Inscriptions on his statues record temple building and dedications to deities.
Sponsored the rebuilding of temples and commissioned inscribed statues for them.
His monuments preserve evidence of Sumerian government, religion and language.
hatshepsut: Hatshepsut adopted royal titles while sharing power with Thutmose III. Her monuments portray her with Egyptian royal dress and insignia.
Adopted the full royal titulary and the throne name Maatkare, and commissioned royal monuments.
Her monuments document a woman's exercise of kingship and the presentation of royal legitimacy.
jahangir: Jahangir valued precise portraits and depictions of nature, encouraging studies of plants and animals.
Supported portraiture, natural studies and distinctive approaches among court artists.
His patronage advanced Mughal painting and recognition of individual artists.
labille_guiard: Adélaïde Labille-Guiard joined the French Royal Academy in 1783 and exhibited her portrait with two pupils in 1785, when women's membership was restricted.
Exhibited at the Salon, taught women artists and presented herself as a professional painter and teacher.
Her work documents women's artistic education and has been interpreted as advocating their professional standing.
rembrandt: Rembrandt made self-portraits throughout his life. In his 1660 portrait, layers of paint convey his face and signs of ageing.
Produced many self-portraits and explored light and paint texture in portraiture.
His work offers insight into artistic self-representation and the portrait market.
senwosret_iii: Twelfth Dynasty; approximately nineteenth century BCE
Senusret III strengthened royal authority and Egyptian control in Nubia. His statues often show mature features and heavy eyelids.
Consolidated royal power; Egyptian influence in Nubia was supported by military fortresses.
His statues show how portraiture presented a mature ruler with political strength.
shah_jahan: Reign: 1628–1658 CE, following the Met source
Shah Jahan commissioned the Taj Mahal as his wife's mausoleum and founded Shahjahanabad in Delhi.
Commissioned major building projects and the illustrated history of his reign, the Padshahnama.
His projects left major architectural monuments and a distinctive court image of authority.
thutmose_iii: Thutmose III became king as a child and shared power with Hatshepsut. He later led campaigns in the Levant and reached the Euphrates.
Led campaigns in Palestine and Syria and expanded temples in Egypt and Nubia, including Karnak.
Extended Egyptian influence; Karnak inscriptions record his campaigns and temple gifts.
ur_ningirsu: An inscription identifies Ur-Ningirsu as ruler of Lagash and Gudea's son, and records the dedication of his statue to his personal deity.
Succeeded Gudea and dedicated an inscribed statue bearing his name and lineage.
The statue documents royal succession and the continuing tradition of dedicatory royal sculpture.
alexander: Alexander led campaigns beyond Macedonia deep into Asia before dying in Babylon. Many surviving representations of him were made after his death.
Led extensive military expansion; his royal image featured a clean-shaven face and diadem.
His visual model influenced Hellenistic kings and later rulers.
darius_i: Darius I governed the Achaemenid Empire and developed its administration and communications.
Supported roads and provincial government and began royal projects at Susa and Persepolis.
Helped consolidate the administration of a large, diverse empire.
justinian_i: Justinian ruled the Eastern Roman Empire in the sixth century, combining military campaigns with legal reforms and building projects.
Sponsored the compilation of Roman civil law and the rebuilding of Hagia Sophia in 532–537.
His legal compilation and architecture influenced later centuries.
ibn_al_haytham: Born in Basra and active in Cairo, Ibn al-Haytham studied light and vision, combining mathematical analysis with experiments.
Investigated reflection and refraction and tested explanations of sight.
Latin translations of his optical works contributed to later studies of light and vision.
suleiman_i: Ottoman influence expanded under Suleiman I, while court arts and architecture flourished. His title 'the Lawgiver' reflects his association with legal reforms.
Supported legal reforms and architectural projects, including works by Sinan.
His reign left a lasting mark on administration, art and architecture.
wu_zetian: Reign with the imperial title: 690–705 CE
Wu Zetian rose within the Tang court, declared herself emperor in 690 and established the Zhou dynasty.
Held the imperial title directly after years of political influence at court.
Her rule was an exceptional case in the history of Chinese imperial government.
hokusai: Hokusai worked in ukiyo-e, producing drawings and woodblock prints. The Great Wave belongs to his Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji.
Designed the Mount Fuji series and explored colour printing in landscapes.
His work became a prominent example of Japanese printmaking in the Edo period.
sejong: Alphabet created in 1443; explanation published in 1446 CE
Sejong is associated with the creation of Hunminjeongeum, now called Hangul. The 1446 book explains the alphabet's purpose and design.
Created the Korean letters, with court scholars explaining and documenting the system.
Provided a system for writing Korean sounds and preserved an explanation of its principles.
ashoka: Ashoka ruled large parts of the Indian subcontinent and supported Buddhism. His rock and pillar edicts describe ethical and administrative concerns.
Issued edicts addressing moral conduct and the welfare of humans and animals.
His inscriptions preserve a comparatively direct royal voice on government and ethics in ancient India.
jayavarman_vii: Accession: 1181; late twelfth–early thirteenth centuries CE
Jayavarman VII became king in 1181 and is associated with Angkor Thom and major temple projects.
Founded Angkor Thom and sponsored temples and care institutions, including hospitals recorded in inscriptions.
His projects provide major evidence of Khmer kingship and Buddhist architecture.
lady_xook: Documented activity in the eighth century CE; a monument dated 709
Lady K'abal Xook appears on Yaxchilan monuments with her husband, Shield Jaguar, participating in rituals linked to royal authority.
Performed royal ritual roles recorded on carved lintels.
Her monuments help illuminate women's roles in Maya political and ritual life.
moctezuma_ii: Reign: 1502–1520 CE, following the exhibition source
Moctezuma II ruled from Tenochtitlan with political, military and ritual authority. His final years coincided with the arrival of Cortés and his allies.
Administered a large state and its military and ritual institutions.
His life helps explain the Mexica state and the upheaval surrounding the Spanish conquest.
pachacuti: Pachacuti is associated with the expansion of Cusco into the Inca empire and the reorganization of its capital.
Led Inca expansion and reshaped Cusco as a political and ritual centre.
Prepared the way for further imperial expansion in the Andes.
taharqa: Taharqa ruled Kush and Egypt in the seventh century BCE, leaving inscriptions, statues and building projects.
Sponsored temple construction and additions at Kawa and sites in Egypt.
His monuments reveal political and religious connections between Kush and Egypt.
menelik_ii: Late nineteenth century; Battle of Adwa, 1896 CE
Menelik II led Ethiopian forces against the Italian army at Adwa in 1896.
Led the resistance that defeated the Italian campaign at Adwa.
The victory became a symbol of resistance to colonialism and Ethiopian independence.
mansa_musa: Reign: 1312–approximately 1337 CE, following the museum source
Mansa Musa became famous for his pilgrimage in the 1320s and his expenditure of gold along the route.
Strengthened Mali's presence in trans-Saharan networks through travel and exchange.
Accounts of his journey and later maps spread awareness of Mali and its wealth.
idia: Idia was the mother of King Esigie. Court traditions credit her with important political advice, and her son created the office of queen mother for her.
Helped consolidate her son's rule through counsel and gained an official court position.
Became a model for the political and ritual role of the queen mother in Benin.
kamehameha_i: Kamehameha I is associated with the unification of the Hawaiian islands and the founding of the kingdom.
United the islands into one kingdom and made Kamakahonu a residence late in his life.
His reign formed a foundational period in the kingdom's political history.
raden_saleh: Nineteenth century; reached the Netherlands in 1829 and returned to Java in 1851
Raden Saleh came from a prominent Javanese family and travelled to the Netherlands to study painting.
Developed a painting practice across European and Javanese artistic and social settings.
His life offers a way to study artistic exchange and identity under colonialism.
greek_sphinx: Artistic witness: a painting dated 1864 CE, not the origin of the myth
In the Oedipus story, the Sphinx challenges travellers with a riddle. Moreau's painting depicts the confrontation, a Greek myth revisited in later European art.
Not a historical achievement; its narrative role is described here.
Represents danger and the testing of knowledge, and inspired later artists.
griffin: Artistic witness: 1250–1300 CE, not the origin of the myth
In the Byzantine context described by the museum, the griffin is a guardian and symbol of authority. The reference marble panel may have belonged to a tomb, but this is uncertain.
Not a historical achievement; its narrative role is described here.
Associated with guardianship, authority and funerary symbolism.
japanese_dragon: Artistic witness: probably eighteenth or early nineteenth century CE
The museum account connects dragons in Japanese art with water and rain. The reference artwork shows a dragon in clouds during the Edo period.
Not a historical achievement; its narrative role is described here.
A symbol associated with water and rain in the cited tradition.
lamassu: Assyrian lamassu sculptures guarded important palace entrances. In the cited example, five legs make the figure appear stationary from the front and walking from the side.
Not a historical achievement; its cultural role is described here.
Protected entrances symbolically and expressed royal power and prestige.
makara_java: Archaeological witness: approximately tenth century CE
Museum accounts connect the makara with water and temple entrances in Central Java. The reference object is a stone waterspout.
Not a historical achievement; its cultural role is described here.
Connects water, architectural decoration and symbolic guardianship.
simurgh: In the story of Zal, the Simurgh rescues the abandoned child and raises him in its nest.
Not a historical achievement; its narrative role is described here.
Represents care and protection in Zal's story and inspired manuscript illustrations.
qilin: The qilin's appearance is associated with good government. Some depictions connect a carried book with the announcement of a scholar's birth.
Not a historical achievement; its narrative role is described here.
A symbol of benevolence, wisdom and auspicious events.
haetae: The haetae appears in Korean art, including a Buddhist drum stand in the national museum. Seoul's cultural account associates it with justice and protection.
Not a historical achievement; its cultural role is described here.
Served as a guardian symbol in art and inspired Seoul's modern emblem.
garuda_nepal: A Nepalese object dated 1004 shows Garuda carrying Vishnu. Garuda also appears in South Asian royal symbolism.
Not a historical achievement; its cultural role is described here.
Vishnu's carrier, with religious and royal associations.
pegasus: Reference cup: late fifth century BCE
In the myth, Bellerophon rides Pegasus against the Chimera. The story appears in ancient Corinthian art and on a silver cup in the Met.
Not a historical achievement; its narrative role is described here.
A figure in Greek heroic storytelling and art.
ammit: Ancient Egypt; no origin date established in this research
In Egyptian beliefs about judgement after death, Ammit devours the heart that fails the weighing. Funerary images place her beside the scales.
Not a historical achievement; its cultural role is described here.
Embodies the consequences of failing the moral judgement of the dead.
taniwha: Multiple traditions with no single origin date
Taniwha stories vary among Māori communities. Some describe guardians, others water-related dangers; no single appearance applies to every story.
Not a historical achievement; its narrative role is described here.
Connects places, water, protection and danger in Māori traditions.
ibn_sina: Ibn Sina was a physician and philosopher raised in the Samanid environment of Bukhara. He wrote on medicine, logic and philosophy.
Authored The Canon of Medicine and The Book of Healing and developed a comprehensive philosophical system.
His work influenced philosophy and science in the Islamic world for centuries, prompting extensive commentary and debate.
al_kindi: Al-Kindi was an Arab philosopher active in Abbasid Baghdad, writing on philosophy, mathematics, optics and music.
Helped bring Greek learning into Arabic intellectual life and develop Arabic scientific and philosophical terminology.
His work supported later intellectual debates, with some influence reaching Europe through Latin translations.
al_jahiz: Al-Jahiz grew up in Basra and also worked in Baghdad. His prose combines observation, argument and many fields of knowledge.
Wrote The Book of Animals and Al-Bayan wa al-Tabyin, exploring nature, knowledge, language and rhetoric.
Influenced Arabic prose through rhetorical skill, varied subjects and social observation.
al_mutanabbi: Al-Mutanabbi was born in Kufa and travelled among courts, notably that of Sayf al-Dawla in Aleppo.
Composed major praise poems, many connected with Sayf al-Dawla.
His widely quoted poetry remains prominent in Arabic literary culture.
nazik_al_malaika: Nazik al-Malaika was an Iraqi poet born in Baghdad, a comparative-literature scholar and university teacher, and a pioneer of Arabic free verse.
Wrote Cholera and experimented with forms that expanded modern Arabic poetry.
Her work helped establish the place of free verse in Arabic literature.
badr_al_sayyab: Badr Shakir al-Sayyab came from Jaykur south of Basra and helped renew Arabic poetry as a pioneer of free verse.
Experimented with poetic structure and used myths of renewal and rebirth.
Helped develop modern Arabic poetry and its use of symbolism and myth.
zaha_hadid: Zaha Hadid was born in Baghdad, studied architecture in London and established her practice there, working on buildings, urban space and interiors.
Designed the Vitra Fire Station and Rosenthal Center, and became the first woman to receive the Pritzker Prize in 2004.
Expanded architectural experimentation with forms and urban spaces worldwide.
ramesses_ii: Ramesses II ruled New Kingdom Egypt. His reign is associated with large royal projects and the expression of authority through buildings and statues.
Associated with the rock-cut temples of Abu Simbel in the thirteenth century BCE.
His monuments remain important evidence of Egyptian construction and royal art.
hammurabi: Reign: 1792–1750 BCE, following the Louvre chronology
Hammurabi was a Babylonian king associated with a legal stele showing him with the god Shamash.
Sponsored a collection of legal rulings inscribed on the stele now in the Louvre.
The monument helps explain justice, authority and law in Old Babylonian society.
marcus_aurelius: Marcus Aurelius was a Roman emperor whose personal writings, known as Meditations, explore philosophy and self-discipline.
Left Meditations and established teaching chairs for philosophical schools in Athens.
His writings became a major source for philosophy as a daily practice, particularly Stoicism.
babur: Babur was a Central Asian prince who founded Mughal rule in India and recorded his life and surroundings in memoirs.
Established the dynasty in 1526 and wrote memoirs in Chagatai Turkish, later translated into Persian under Akbar.
Founded a state with a major impact on South Asian history; his memoirs illuminate his era.
leonardo_da_vinci: Leonardo was a Renaissance artist who combined painting with anatomy, engineering and observations of nature.
Painted the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper and left extensive notebooks of drawings and observations.
His treatment of expression and composition influenced artists, while his notebooks connect art with inquiry.
george_washington: Washington commanded the Continental Army, presided over the Constitutional Convention and became the first United States president.
Combined military leadership with a role in establishing republican institutions.
Helped shape the presidency and the emerging state; his life also included enslaving people.
aristotle: Aristotle studied at Plato's Academy, investigated philosophy, living things and politics, and tutored Alexander.
Developed influential works on logic, ethics, politics and nature.
Became one of antiquity's most influential thinkers in philosophy and science.
cyrus_ii: Cyrus II was a Persian ruler who founded the Achaemenid Empire in the sixth century BCE.
Brought extensive territories under Achaemenid rule; royal inscriptions record his name and lineage.
Laid the foundations of a major power in the ancient Near East.
theodora_i: Theodora, wife of Justinian I, exercised influence in the Byzantine court and state.
Historical accounts credit her with urging Justinian to stand firm during the Nika revolt in 532.
Her life illustrates women's exercise of power at the Byzantine court.
al_biruni: Al-Biruni was a scholar from Khwarazm who worked in astronomy, mathematics and measurement, combining observation with theory.
Calculated latitudes and investigated astronomical, mathematical and historical questions.
His work connects observation, mathematics and the study of societies in medieval Islamic scholarship.
mehmed_ii: Mehmed II was an Ottoman sultan who ruled in two periods and captured Constantinople in 1453.
Led the siege, expanded Ottoman rule and sponsored institutions and building projects.
The conquest reshaped regional power and the centre of the Ottoman state.
confucius: Confucius was a Chinese thinker concerned with education, ethics, ritual and good government in the late Zhou period.
His disciples transmitted ideas on conduct and social relationships, including those preserved in the Analects.
Became a central reference in East Asian intellectual, educational and political traditions.
murasaki_shikibu: Murasaki Shikibu was a writer at the Heian court, associated with The Tale of Genji and its portrayals of court society.
Wrote The Tale of Genji, one of Japan's best-known literary works.
The tale inspired painting, calligraphy, dress and other arts into modern culture.
yi_sun_sin: Yi Sun-sin was a Korean commander who resisted the Japanese invasions of 1592–1598 and kept a military diary.
Led naval operations and recorded warfare, feelings, weather and daily conditions in Nanjung Ilgi.
His diary provides direct evidence of naval warfare and a sixteenth-century commander's experience.
rabindranath_tagore: Tagore was a Bengali writer whose work includes poetry, songs, stories, plays and social reflections.
Received the 1913 Nobel Prize in Literature and established an experimental school at Santiniketan in 1901.
Reached a global readership and contributed to debates about education and Indian and Western cultures.
suryavarman_ii: Twelfth century; Angkor Wat construction: 1113–1150, according to APSARA
Suryavarman II was a Khmer king associated with Angkor Wat as a royal temple and centre of authority.
Sponsored Angkor Wat; its reliefs commemorate events of his reign.
Left a major architectural and religious legacy in Khmer and Cambodian history.
kinich_janaab_pakal: Pakal was a Maya ruler whose name and life dates appear in inscriptions. His tomb was found in Palenque's Temple of the Inscriptions.
Palenque flourished under his rule, and his funerary temple was begun late in his life.
His monuments provide important evidence of Maya authority, chronology and art.
nezahualcoyotl: Nezahualcoyotl ruled Texcoco and is associated with an alliance with the Mexica and a Nahuatl poetic and intellectual tradition.
Recovered Texcoco's throne; poems reflecting on life and its passing are attributed to him.
Represents Texcoco's political and literary traditions and their links to the pre-conquest Nahua world.
tupac_inca_yupanqui: Reign: 1471–1493 CE, following the Smithsonian source
Tupac Inca Yupanqui commanded armies under his father Pachacuti, then continued expansion as ruler.
Extended the empire and Qhapaq Ñan road network southward, with expansion also reaching the coasts of Peru and Ecuador.
Helped connect an expanding empire by roads, through conquest that also subjugated other peoples.
amanirenas: Amanirenas was a Kushite queen named in a Meroitic inscription and associated with conflict against Rome in Nubia.
Kush resisted Roman expansion during her reign; subsequent agreements preserved Meroitic authority over the remaining Nubian territory.
Her life illustrates queenship in Kush and its political survival against Rome.
lalibela: Lalibela was an Ethiopian king associated with the rock-hewn church complex in the city bearing his name.
Tradition credits him with sponsoring churches conceived as a holy city and an alternative pilgrimage destination to Jerusalem.
The site remains a centre of pilgrimage and evidence of Ethiopian Christian architecture.
askia_muhammad: Askia Muhammad was a Songhai ruler associated with Gao and Islamic architectural heritage in the West African Sahel.
UNESCO attributes the construction of the Tomb of Askia complex at Gao to him.
His legacy reflects Songhai power, trans-Saharan trade and Islamic traditions.
ewuare_i: Ewuare was an Edo ruler associated with strengthening Benin and developing its court and royal symbolism.
Traditions credit him with administrative changes, palace building, fortifications and support for arts and ritual.
Helped consolidate the oba's authority and the symbolic language of Benin royal art.
liliuokalani: Nineteenth–early twentieth centuries; queen from 1891, overthrown in 1893
Liliʻuokalani opposed the overthrow of the Hawaiian monarchy and annexation, defending her people's rights.
Sought to restore the kingdom's authority and left writings on Hawaiian history and heritage.
Remains a symbol of Hawaiian sovereignty and cultural memory.
kartini: Kartini was a Javanese writer whose letters discussed education, marriage and women's rights under colonial rule.
Advocated girls' education and expressed ideas for social reform in her letters.
Her letters influenced debates on education and equality and inspired educational institutions in Indonesia.
jawad_selim: Jawad Saleem helped develop Iraqi modern art and sculpture teaching in Baghdad, combining artistic heritage with contemporary expression.
Established the sculpture department at the Institute of Fine Arts, helped found the Baghdad Modern Art Group and designed the Freedom Monument.
Influenced arts education, public sculpture and modern Iraqi artistic identity.
sima_qian: Sima Qian was a Chinese historian associated with the Shiji, or Records of the Grand Historian.
Compiled a wide-ranging account of Chinese history in the Shiji.
The structure of his work influenced later Chinese histories.
matsuo_basho: Matsuo Bashō was an Edo-period poet known for short poetry and literary journeys.
Developed haikai and hokku traditions and taught poetry.
Became an influential reference in Japanese short-poetry traditions.
anna_komnene: Anna Komnene, daughter of Emperor Alexios I, wrote the Alexiad about her father's reign.
Authored the Alexiad, an important source for the period.
Preserved a Byzantine account of political and military events and contact with the First Crusade.
shin_saimdang: Shin Saimdang was a Korean artist associated with painting, calligraphy and poetry, and the mother of the thinker Yi I.
Became known for depictions of nature, including plants and insects.
Remains prominent in Korean artistic and cultural memory.
indravarman_i: Ninth century CE; Bakong consecrated in 881
Indravarman I's reign is associated with temple projects at Hariharalaya, in today's Roluos area.
Sponsored Preah Ko and Bakong, major examples of early Khmer architecture.
His projects helped develop the royal temple-mountain tradition.
piye: Piye was a Kushite king based at Napata, in present-day Sudan, whose dynasty extended its influence north into Egypt.
Campaigned in Egypt, captured Memphis and returned to Napata.
Kushite expansion prepared the way for Egypt's Twenty-fifth Dynasty.
zewditu: Zewditu, daughter of Menelik II, held the throne while Ras Tafari served as heir and regent.
Ruled during a period of shared authority with Tafari, later known as Haile Selassie.
Her reign reveals struggles over power and change in early twentieth-century Ethiopia.
sunni_ali: Sunni Ali expanded Songhai power in the Niger River region of West Africa.
Extended control over cities and trading centres, including Timbuktu.
Helped establish a major regional power along West African trade routes.
esigie: Esigie was an Edo ruler of the Kingdom of Benin, in present-day Nigeria.
Consolidated royal authority after a succession struggle and honoured his mother Idia with the position of queen mother.
His reign is associated with the queen mother's status and royal arts and rituals.
pomare_iv: Pōmare IV ruled Tahiti during growing tensions with France and the imposition of a French protectorate.
Resisted French intervention, then returned to Papeete in 1847 under the protectorate.
Her reign reflects Tahiti's transition to sovereignty constrained by colonial protection.
hayam_wuruk: Hayam Wuruk was a Javanese king associated with the flourishing of the Majapahit court.
The Nagarakretagama poem, composed in his honour, records his journeys and court.
The text provides important evidence for the state and society of historical Java.
pliny_elder: Pliny the Elder wrote Natural History, an encyclopaedia gathering knowledge and accounts from the ancient world.
Compiled extensive material on nature, geography and the arts from earlier works.
Preserved ancient knowledge and influenced its reception in later periods.
ashurbanipal: Reign: 668–631 BCE, following the Yale project
Ashurbanipal was an Assyrian king associated with cuneiform tablet collections at Nineveh, near modern Mosul.
Sponsored the collection of varied texts in Nineveh's palace libraries.
The surviving collections preserve Mesopotamian literature and knowledge for modern study.
enheduanna: Enheduanna was Sargon's daughter and high priestess of Nanna at Ur. An archaeological disk records her name, position and symbolic image.
Her name is associated with Sumerian hymns, including the Exaltation of Inanna, while monuments document her religious role.
An important figure in the history of authorship, the reception of Sumerian literature and women's institutional roles.
anzu: Attested in tradition from at least the third millennium BCE, according to ORACC
Anzû is a hybrid being, depicted here as a lion-headed bird. Mesopotamian literature associates it with mountains; Assyrian art at Kalhu shows it confronting Ninurta.
Not a historical achievement; its narrative role is described here.
A figure in Mesopotamian mythology and religious imagery.
al_khwarizmi: Active in the first half of the ninth century CE
Al-Khwarizmi worked in Baghdad in connection with the Abbasid court and wrote on algebra, arithmetic, astronomy and geography.
Authored a treatise on algebra and works on calculation, astronomical tables and geography.
His works and translations helped transmit methods of calculation and algebra across scholarly traditions.
hypatia: Hypatia taught in Alexandria and was associated with Neoplatonism, mathematics and astronomy.
Taught mathematics and philosophy; her student Synesius's letters document her scholarly standing.
Contributed to the transmission of philosophical and mathematical education in late antiquity.
aryabhata_i: Active in the late fifth–early sixth centuries CE
Aryabhata authored the Aryabhatiya, a Sanskrit text combining mathematics and astronomy.
Completed it in 499 and explained apparent daily celestial motion through the Earth's rotation.
Influenced Indian astronomical and mathematical commentaries, with his tradition also reaching the Islamic world.
euclid: Euclid was a scholar of Greek culture who worked in Alexandria and became known for the Elements.
Organized a wide body of mathematics and proofs, drawing on earlier work.
The Elements became a long-lasting reference for geometry and deductive reasoning.
zhang_heng: Zhang Heng was an Eastern Han scholar and writer who held a scientific court office and wrote on astronomy.
Associated with an instrument for detecting earthquakes and their direction, and instruments representing the heavens.
An early contributor to the combination of astronomical observation and scientific instruments in China.
seondeok: Seondeok was the first woman to rule Silla, during competition among the Korean kingdoms.
Her reign is associated with projects including Cheomseongdae and the pagoda at Hwangnyongsa.
Represents an important period in women's rule and Buddhist architectural patronage in Silla.
horemheb: Reign: approximately 1323–1309 BCE, following the Met exhibition
Horemheb was a royal scribe and army commander under Tutankhamun before becoming the last king of the Eighteenth Dynasty.
Issued legislation described by the museum as limiting military power and protecting civilian rights.
His reign marked a political and religious transition at the end of the dynasty.
te_puea_herangi: Te Puea Hērangi was a social and political leader who strengthened the Māori King movement and helped rebuild Waikato communities.
Led the establishment of Tūrangawaewae and supported land development, farming and community care.
Strengthened Kīngitanga and Tainui communities' capacity to organize and recover from land confiscation.
njinga_mbandi: Njinga combined negotiation, alliances and warfare in response to Portuguese expansion in west-central Africa.
Became ruler of Ndongo in 1624 and later ruled Matamba, pursuing alliances and negotiations to maintain her authority.
Became prominent in Angolan historical memory and the history of African women's leadership.
sequoyah: Sequoyah developed a syllabary for the Cherokee language rather than reducing it to a Latin alphabet.
The Cherokee council adopted his completed system in 1821, after which literacy in it spread.
The system became important for language preservation, education and written expression.
sor_juana: Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz wrote Spanish-language poetry, drama and prose in the Baroque culture of New Spain.
Wrote First Dream, plays and the Reply to Sor Filotea.
Left a major legacy in Mexican and Spanish literature and women's intellectual history.
jose_rizal: José Rizal was a Filipino intellectual who criticized colonial oppression through writing and became a major national figure.
Wrote Noli Me Tangere and El Filibusterismo, novels addressing colonial repression.
His writings and life helped shape Filipino national consciousness and remain part of education.
wilma_mankiller: Wilma Mankiller became the first woman principal chief of the Cherokee Nation after working in community development.
Served as deputy chief, became principal chief in 1985 and pursued community-development projects.
Expanded women's leadership and strengthened Cherokee community action and self-government.
andres_bonifacio: Andrés Bonifacio was central to the Katipunan and the Philippine revolutionary movement against Spanish rule.
Helped found the Katipunan in 1892 and lead the revolution in 1896.
Became a prominent symbol of the struggle for Philippine independence.
ibn_battuta: Active in the fourteenth century CE
Ibn Battuta was a traveller from Tangier associated with a wide-ranging account of journeys through Africa, Asia and other regions.
Dictated travel material composed by Ibn Juzayy, preserving descriptions of cities, customs, rulers and routes.
The Rihla became an important source for connections among fourteenth-century societies.
al_idrisi: Twelfth century; geographical work completed in 1154 CE
Al-Idrisi worked at Roger II's Sicilian court, gathering geographical knowledge from texts and travellers' accounts.
Prepared Nuzhat al-Mushtaq and the maps associated with Roger II.
His work brought together Arabic and Mediterranean geographical knowledge.
ban_zhao: Active in the late first–early second centuries CE
Ban Zhao was an Eastern Han writer associated with the history of Han and Lessons for Women.
Contributed to the Han shu and wrote lessons on women's education and social conduct.
Her text remained influential in discussions of women's education and roles in Chinese traditions.
sappho: Active in the late seventh–early sixth centuries BCE
Sappho was a Greek poet from Lesbos whose work survives largely in fragments and quotations.
Created lyric poetry about emotion, relationships and human experience.
Her poetry has continued to influence literature, translation and scholarship.
maria_sibylla_merian: Maria Sibylla Merian studied insects, their development and their relationships with plants through observation and drawing.
Studied Suriname's natural world and published Metamorphosis of the Insects of Suriname in 1705.
Contributed influential images and observations to the study of insect life cycles and scientific illustration.
josefa_de_obidos: Josefa de Óbidos was born in Seville and worked in Portugal, becoming known for still lifes and religious paintings.
Created detailed religious works and still lifes with Baroque symbolism.
Her paintings illuminate seventeenth-century Portuguese art and women's participation in artistic production.
piri_reis: Active in the late fifteenth–first half of the sixteenth century
Piri Reis was an Ottoman navigator who combined seafaring experience with geographical sources in maps and sailing guides.
Produced the 1513 world map and the Kitab-ı Bahriye on Mediterranean ports and coasts.
Preserved Ottoman nautical knowledge and evidence of the circulation of information about the Atlantic.
tycho_brahe: Tycho Brahe was a Danish astronomer who made precise observations before telescopes were used in astronomy.
Developed systematic observations using large instruments and left data later used by Johannes Kepler.
His observations contributed to Kepler's formulation of the laws of planetary motion.
jang_yeong_sil: Active in the fifteenth century; clock of 1434 CE
Jang Yeong-sil was an instrument maker at the Joseon court associated with an automatically striking water clock.
Produced the Jagyeongnu time-announcing clock in 1434 through work sponsored by Sejong.
Contributed to timekeeping and scientific instruments in Joseon.
zheng_he: Zheng He was a Ming naval commander who led diplomatic, commercial and military voyages across the Indian Ocean.
Led voyages reaching South and Southeast Asian ports and the East African coast.
Strengthened maritime connections, political influence and exchange between China and Indian Ocean societies.
